## Faust: Exporting {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- Faust manages to **export** an audio program to many different platforms thanks to its ***architecture file system***.
- Every single **export target** is materialized by a **specific architecture file**, **written in C++**.
:::
- The architecture file is **completely generic**, it doesn't change depending on the Faust program.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="1-5|7-11|13-14|16-18|19-21|23-26|28-30|32-33|35-38" filename="faust/architecture/pa-gtk.cpp"}
// Include code from the faust and portaudio C++ libraries:
#include "faust/gui/FUI.h"
#include "faust/misc.h"
#include "faust/audio/portaudio-dsp.h"
#include "faust/gui/GTKUI.h"

// These are markers used to indicate to the Faust compiler
// where to 'paste' the generated DSP code
// from the .dsp file
<<includeIntrinsic>>
<<includeclass>>

// Create a DSP object
mydsp DSP;

// Program entrypoint:
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
  // Build the GTK User Interface:
  GUI* interface = new GTKUI (appname, &argc, &argv);
  DSP.buildUserInterface(interface);

  // Get the sample-rate from command-line arguments:
  long srate = (long)lopt(argv, "--sample-rate", 44100);
  // Get the buffer size from command-line arguments:
  int fpb = lopt(argv, "--buffer", 128);

  // Create the portaudio backend and initialize it:
  portaudio audio(srate, fpb);
  audio.init(appname, &DSP);

  // Run the interface:
  interface->run();

  // When the GTK Interface is closed, stop the audio
  // and deallocate the interface.  
  audio.stop();
  delete interface;
}
```

- The architecture file is **completely generic**, it doesn't change depending on the Faust program.
:::
- Instead, the **generated C++ code** for the **DSP program** is going to be inserted inside the architecture file, to create the **final compilable file**.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="1-5|7-10|12|14-20|23|25-30|32-60|62-64|66-69|71-82|" filename="fm.cpp"}
/* ------------------------------------------------------------
name: "fm"
Code generated with Faust 2.88.0 (https://faust.grame.fr)
Compilation options: -lang cpp -fpga-mem-th 4 -ct 1 -es 1 -mcd 16 -mdd 1024 -mdy 33 -single -ftz 0
------------------------------------------------------------ */

#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdint>
#include <math.h>

class mydsp : public dsp {
private:
  int fSampleRate;
  float fConst0;
  float fConst1;
  float fRec2[2];
  float fConst2;
  float fRec1[2];
  float fRec0[2];
	
public:
  mydsp() {}

  virtual int getNumInputs() {
 	return 0;
  }
  virtual int getNumOutputs() {
 	return 1;
  }

  virtual void instanceConstants(int sample_rate) {
 	fSampleRate = sample_rate;
 	fConst0 = std::min<float>(1.92e+05f, std::max<float>(1.0f, static_cast<float>(fSampleRate)));
 	fConst1 = 4.4e+02f / fConst0;
 	fConst2 = 1.0f / fConst0;
  }

  virtual void instanceClear() {
 	for (int l0 = 0; l0 < 2; l0 = faust_wrap_add(l0, 1)) {
  		fRec2[l0] = 0.0f;
 	}
 	for (int l1 = 0; l1 < 2; l1 = faust_wrap_add(l1, 1)) {
  		fRec1[l1] = 0.0f;
 	}
 	for (int l2 = 0; l2 < 2; l2 = faust_wrap_add(l2, 1)) {
  		fRec0[l2] = 0.0f;
 	}
  }

  virtual void init(int sample_rate) {
 	classInit(sample_rate);
 	instanceInit(sample_rate);
  }

  virtual void instanceInit(int sample_rate) {
 	instanceConstants(sample_rate);
 	instanceResetUserInterface();
 	instanceClear();
  }

  virtual int getSampleRate() {
 	return fSampleRate;
  }

  virtual void buildUserInterface(UI* ui_interface) {
 	ui_interface->openVerticalBox("fm");
 	ui_interface->closeBox();
  }

  virtual void compute(int count, FAUSTFLOAT** RESTRICT inputs, FAUSTFLOAT** RESTRICT outputs) {
 	FAUSTFLOAT* output0 = outputs[0];
 	for (int i0 = 0; i0 < count; i0 = faust_wrap_add(i0, 1)) {
  		fRec2[0] = fConst1 - std::floor(fRec2[1]) + fRec2[1];
  		float fTemp0 = 4.4e+02f + 1.32e+03f * std::cos(6.2831855f * fRec2[1]);
  		fRec1[0] = fRec1[1] + fConst2 * fTemp0 - std::floor(fRec1[1]);
  		fRec0[0] = fRec0[1] + fConst2 * (4.4e+02f + 2.0f * fTemp0 * std::cos(6.2831855f * fRec1[1])) - std::floor(fRec0[1]);
  		output0[i0] = static_cast<FAUSTFLOAT>(std::cos(6.2831855f * fRec0[1]));
  		fRec2[1] = fRec2[0];
  		fRec1[1] = fRec1[0];
  		fRec0[1] = fRec0[0];
 	}
  }
};
```

- `struct` functions are declared with the syntax: `type myfunction()`. They are called ***methods***. The type represents **the value they return** after executing their instructions.

## Faust: Anatomy of a C++ audio program {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- A **C/C++** `struct` represents a named data structure, in which one can **store data** of different types, and define **functions** associated (or not) with that data.
- Stored data can be **declared** with the syntax: `type mydata`. They are called **`struct` members.**
- `struct` functions are declared with the syntax: `type myfunction()`. They are called ***methods***. The type represents **the value they return** after executing their instructions.
:::
- We can **define what a method does** by opening a **curly-braces** `{}` **scope** after its name.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="13-24|14-16|17-21|22-23,1|24,13|" filename="sinewave.cpp"}
#include <cmath>

struct Sinewave {
    // Stored data: 32-bits floating-point value:
    float phase;

    // Initialization function declaration:
    void init() {
        phase = 0;
    }

    // Processing function declaration:
    float process() {
        // Increment phase sample-by-sample
        // for a fixed frequency of 440 Hz
        phase += 440.f / 48000.f;
        // When phase reaches its maximum (1.0),
        // start from 0.0 again:
        if (phase >= 1.f) {
            phase -= 1.f;
        }
        // Compute and return the sinewave value:
        float sine = sin(phase * 2.f * M_PI);
        return sine;
    }
};
```

## Faust: Anatomy of a C++ audio program {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
:::
- The `int main()` function is the ***entrypoint of a program***, it is the first function that is executed. It should **always return an integer value at the end**, either `0` if the program exited successfully, or otherwise an arbitrary **error code**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="28-30" filename="sinewave.cpp"}
#include <cmath>

struct Sinewave {
    // Stored data: 32-bits floating-point value:
    float phase;

    // Initialization function declaration:
    void init() {
        phase = 0;
    }

    // Processing function declaration:
    float process() {
        // Increment phase sample-by-sample
        // for a fixed frequency of 440 Hz
        phase += 440.f / 48000.f;
        // When phase reaches its maximum (1.0),
        // start from 0.0 again:
        if (phase >= 1.f) {
            phase -= 1.f;
        }
        // Compute and return the sinewave value:
        float sine = sin(phase * 2.f * M_PI);
        return sine;
    }
};

int main() {
    return 0;
}
```

## Faust: Anatomy of a C++ audio program {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- The `int main()` function is the ***entrypoint of a program***, it is the first function that is executed. It should **always return an integer value at the end**, either `0` if the program exited successfully, or otherwise an arbitrary **error code**.
:::
- Inside of it, we can create an instance of our *sinewave* `struct`, store it into a **local variable**, call its *methods*, and visualize the result (**print**).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="30-32|34-35|6,9-11|37-38|14-26|40-41|2|42|" filename="sinewave.cpp"}
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

struct Sinewave {
    // Stored data: 32-bits floating-point value:
    float phase;

    // Initialization function declaration:
    void init() {
        phase = 0;
    }

    // Processing function declaration:
    float process() {
        // Increment phase sample-by-sample
        // for a fixed frequency of 440 Hz
        phase += 440.f / 48000.f;
        // When phase reaches its maximum (1.0),
        // start from 0.0 again:
        if (phase >= 1.f) {
            phase -= 1.f;
        }
        // Compute and return the sinewave value:
        float sine = sin(phase * 2.f * M_PI);
        return sine;
    }
};

int main() {
    // Create an instance of our custom sinewave type,
    // store it into a local variable:
    Sinewave sine;

    // Call its 'init' function:
    sine.init();

    // Get a sample from it, store it in a local variable:
    float sample = sine.process();

    // Print it:
    printf("Sample value: %f", sample);
    return 0;
}
```

## Faust: Anatomy of a C++ audio program {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- The `int main()` function is the ***entrypoint of a program***, it is the first function that is executed. It should **always return an integer value at the end**, either `0` if the program exited successfully, or otherwise an arbitrary **error code**.
- Inside of it, we can create an instance of our *sinewave* `struct`, store it into a **local variable**, call its *methods*, and visualize the result (**print**).
:::
- We can now repeat the process as many times as we want by encapsulating the `process()`and `print()` function calls in a `for` **loop**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="37-41" filename="sinewave.cpp"}
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

struct Sinewave {
    // Stored data: 32-bits floating-point value:
    float phase;

    // Initialization function declaration:
    void init() {
        phase = 0;
    }

    // Processing function declaration:
    float process() {
        // Increment phase sample-by-sample
        // for a fixed frequency of 440 Hz
        phase += 440.f / 48000.f;
        // When phase reaches its maximum (1.0),
        // start from 0.0 again:
        if (phase >= 1.f) {
            phase -= 1.f;
        }
        // Compute and return the sinewave value:
        float sine = sin(phase * 2.f * M_PI);
        return sine;
    }
};

int main() {
    // Create an instance of our custom sinewave type,
    // store it into a local variable:
    Sinewave sine;

    // Call its 'init' function:
    sine.init();

    // Now, the following is going to be repeated 100 times:
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
        float sample = sine.process();
        printf("Sample value: %f\n", sample);
    }
    return 0;
}
```

<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- We could also have made a ***separate structure*** for the '*phase*' computation, to make it **reusable** in other components or **waveform oscillators**.
- Additionally, let's make the **frequency** of the oscillator **variable**, instead of fixed to `440`.
:::
- Now let's make the same `struct` for triangle, sawtooth, and square waves, and let's add an amplitude parameter to them:
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.cpp code-line-numbers="|" filename="sinewave.cpp"}
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

struct Phasor {
    float phase;
    float frequency;

    void init(float freq) {
        phase = 0;
        frequency = freq;
    }

    float process() {
        phase += frequency/48000.f;
        if (phase >= 1.f) {
            phase -= 1.f;
        }
        return phase;
    }
};

struct Sinewave {
    Phasor phasor;

    void init(float freq) {
        phasor.init(freq);
    }

    float process() {
        float phase = phasor.process();
        float sine = sin(phase * M_PI * 2.f);
        return sine;
    }
};

struct Square {
    Phasor phasor;

    void init(float freq) {
        phasor.init(freq);
    }

    float process() {
        float phase = phasor.process();
        float square = phase < 0.5f ? -1.f : 1.f;
        return square;
    }
};

struct Sawtooth {
    Phasor phasor;
    void init(float freq) {
        phasor.init(freq);
    }

    float process() {
        float phase = phasor.process();
        float saw = phase * 2.f - 1.f;
        return saw;
    }
};

struct Triangle {
    Phasor phasor;
    void init(float freq) {
        phasor.init(freq);
    }

    float process() {
        float phase = phasor.process();
        float tri;
        if (phase < 0.5) {
            tri = phase;
        } else {
            tri = 1.f - phase;
        }
        tri -= 0.25;
        tri *= 4.0;
        return tri ;
    }
};

int main() {
    Triangle sine;
    sine.init(440.f);

    for (int i = 0; i < 48000; i++) {
        float sample = sine.process();
        int n = sample * 40 + 40;
        for (int s = 0; s < 100; ++s) {
            if (s == n) {
                printf("%f", sample);
            } else {
                printf(" ");
            }
        }
        printf("\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

```
